analysis.one_liner: Spends hundreds of billions on affordable housing, funded by higher estate taxes on the wealthiest households.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in any of its four committees and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025; all 21 of its supporters were Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would send large sums to build and preserve affordable housing: grants to cities and states to loosen zoning rules that block new homes, tens of billions a year for the national Housing Trust Fund and public housing repairs, and down payment grants of up to 3.5% of a home's value for first-time buyers whose parents never owned a home. It would also restrict how foreclosed government-backed homes get sold, tighten the Community Reinvestment Act's rules for banks, and pay for all of it by raising estate and gift taxes on the largest fortunes. It was referred to four House committees and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and first-generation homebuyers would get new construction grants, down payment assistance, appraisal-gap relief in undervalued neighborhoods, and stronger protections against eviction and predatory land contracts. Public housing residents would see a large one-time capital investment. Construction workers would benefit from prevailing-wage requirements attached to the funds.

how_it_helps.text: Creates competitive grants (authorized at $2 billion a year for 2025-2029) for states, cities, and tribes that reform zoning, allow denser and by-right development, eliminate parking minimums, and adopt tenant protections like just-cause eviction and access to counsel.

Authorizes $44.5 billion a year for 2025-2034 for the Housing Trust Fund, $2.5 billion a year for the Capital Magnet Fund, and a one-time $70 billion for the public housing Capital Fund, plus funding for Indian housing, Native Hawaiian housing, and rural housing programs.
Provides down payment grants of up to 3.5% of a home's appraised value to first-time, first-generation homebuyers with incomes below 120% of area median income (140% in designated high-cost areas).
Creates a $5 billion formula grant program for neighborhoods with an appraisal gap, funding paydowns of arrears, delinquent taxes, and home repairs for borrowers with negative equity.

Requires that at least 75% of single-family homes conveyed to FHA after foreclosure, and at least 90% of properties from sold non-performing loans at FHA, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac, go to owner-occupants or become affordable rental housing for at least 15 years, and bans resale through land installment contracts that don't transfer title.

Expands the Community Reinvestment Act to nonbank mortgage originators, adds penalties for two consecutive failing ratings (including clawback of executive compensation), and deducts financing for fossil fuel expansion from a bank's community-development credit.

Pays for the housing programs through estate and gift tax changes: a surcharge on high-income estates and trusts, a required 10-year minimum term for grantor retained annuity trusts, elimination of the generation-skipping transfer tax exemption for certain transfers, and disallowance of step-up in basis for property held in certain grantor trusts.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy households would pay more in estate and gift taxes under Title IV. Banks and nonbank mortgage companies would face expanded Community Reinvestment Act examinations and new penalties. Investors that buy distressed government-backed mortgages in bulk would face new restrictions on what they can do with the homes.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes very large spending — $44.5 billion a year for the Housing Trust Fund, a single-year $70 billion for public housing capital, and billions more in grant programs — offset by estate tax changes whose revenue depends on wealthy taxpayers' ability to plan around them.

Down payment assistance adds demand to a housing market with a supply shortage, which can push prices up unless the zoning and supply provisions deliver enough new units; eligibility for the down payment grants rests on borrower self-attestation, with no additional documentation required.
The bill touches nearly every part of housing policy at once and was referred to four separate committees, which made it harder to move even for sympathetic members.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs supply-side steps (zoning reform grants, large construction and repair funding) with demand-side help (down payment grants) and pays for it with taxes on the largest estates rather than deficits. The honest trade-offs are cost and execution: the authorized sums are enormous by current housing-program standards, the estate tax offsets are vulnerable to avoidance, and down payment grants could inflate prices if the supply provisions lag. It never got a hearing, so none of these design questions were ever publicly tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced and sent to one subcommittee a month later, and it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Emanuel Cleaver introduced the bill on August 2, 2024, with 20 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The same day, the House referred it to the Financial Services Committee and, additionally, to the Judiciary, Veterans' Affairs, and Ways and Means Committees.
On September 13, 2024, part of the bill was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity; that was the last action of any kind.
No committee scheduled a hearing or markup and the bill never reached the House floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing it automatically.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and nonbank mortgage companies are better off: they will not face the expanded Community Reinvestment Act obligations, penalties, or fossil fuel financing deductions. Wealthy estates avoid the higher estate and gift taxes, and investors that buy distressed government-backed mortgages in bulk keep the current, less restricted rules. Renters and would-be first-generation homebuyers gained nothing.

for.name: Emanuel Cleaver
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which he had championed in earlier Congresses, framing it as making housing more affordable.

for.name: 20 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Jan Schakowsky, Ro Khanna, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ayanna Pressley, and Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors the day the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: First committee of referral, chaired by Patrick McHenry (R)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup during the 118th Congress.

against.name: House Judiciary, Veterans' Affairs, and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Brought no housing legislation of this kind to the floor and allowed the bill to sit in committee until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 supporters — the sponsor and 20 cosponsors — were Democrats, and the bill died in committee in a chamber controlled by Republicans with no Republican cosponsor recorded.

industries.note: The bill expands Community Reinvestment Act coverage to nonbank mortgage companies, adds growth restrictions and executive compensation clawbacks for repeated failing grades, and subtracts fossil fuel expansion financing from community-development credit. These firms' interest in the bill ran against the lower-income communities the Act requires them to serve.

industries.industry: Investors and servicers buying distressed mortgages
industries.note: The bill imposes 90-day borrower notice, mandatory loss mitigation offers, and a requirement that 90% of foreclosed properties from bulk loan sales go to owner-occupants or 15-year affordable rental housing. Investors who profit buying distressed FHA, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac loans would face restrictions they do not have today.
Bank financing of new fossil fuel infrastructure would be deducted from banks' community reinvestment credit, reducing the flow of conventional financing available to fossil fuel expansion projects.

Title IV raises estate and gift taxes: a surcharge on high-income estates, a 10-year minimum for grantor retained annuity trusts, elimination of the generation-skipping transfer exemption for certain transfers, and limits on step-up in basis for grantor trust property. These are the offsets that pay for the housing programs.

Nonprofits, community development financial institutions, and resident councils gain as preferred 'community partners' in government home sales, as eligible builders under the new grant funds, and as recipients of counseling and anti-eviction legal services dollars.

Grant eligibility rewards localities that adopt just-cause eviction, anti-harassment, and rent-stabilization measures, and the bill bans reselling foreclosed homes through land installment contracts without transferring title, tools used by some predatory sellers.

Tens of billions in construction and repair funding plus zoning reform would expand work, but all federally funded construction carries Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirements, raising labor costs on those projects.
